transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-02
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Miles (Redwood), Liam (CISO), Sofia (Cloud Ops), Dev (SRE), Nora (Compliance)

Summary (auto):
High level review of encryption-in-transit and at-rest, BYOK/HSM import path, runbook for crypto handover and forensics post-mortem, audit log retention and RBAC/SSO gating for key access. Agreed to pilot a key-rotation drill and exchange SOC2 material.

Topics: encryption envelope patterns, key hierarchy, HSM import vs cloud-managed KMS, KMS key access policies, emergency key revocation runbook, audit trails for forensics, SSO/SAML + SCIM provisioning for RBAC, data residency concerns.

Transcript:
[00:00:12] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh quick intros, I'm Jordan from Redwood, Priya and Miles are with me.
[00:00:25] Liam: Hi all. Liam, CISO at Ember Energy. We're trying to lock down how we handover keys to Redwood, particularly for the analytics routes that touch PII.
[00:00:34] Priya: great, thanks Liam. To set expectations this is a security deep-dive, we'll cover envelope encryption, KMS integration patterns (AWS KMS/GCP KMS), and HSM import flows — also the runbook for a key compromise scenario.
[00:00:48] Sofia: quick note, our compliance team requires auditable steps for any key operation and we need minimal downtime if we rotate keys.
[00:00:55] Miles: noted — we'll show the approach we recommend and tradeoffs.

[00:01:20] Jordan: first, which model do you want to use primarily — Redwood-hosted keys or BYOK with your own cloud KMS/HSM?
[00:01:28] Dev: our preference is BYOK, we need control and separation. We run on AWS in prod and GCP for analytics, so dual KMS footprints.
[00:01:36] Nora: also the legal team needs proof of custody — chain of custody for any key material.

[00:02:05] Priya: ok, so recommended pattern is envelope encryption: customer master key in your KMS/HSM, data keys generated per model instance and wrapped by that CMK. That way Redwood never stores unwrapped customer master keys.
[00:02:20] Sofia: and for at-rest, are we relying on Redwood's disk encryption plus our wrapped keys?
[00:02:28] Priya: yes. Redwood encrypts persisted model cache, KV cash — sorry, KV cache — and ephemeral checkpoints with data keys. Those data keys are encrypted with your CMK before at-rest. We also use AES-256-GCM with associated data for integrity.
[00:02:45] Jordan: small transcription note — our runtime handles continuous batching and caches, but the important piece is we never persist the plain data key beyond the short lifetime.

[00:03:30] Liam: what about in-transit? mTLS between Redwood and our VPC?
[00:03:35] Miles: yes, we do mutual TLS for private deployment. For hosted API, we rely on TLS 1.3 with cert pinning for the control plane, and optional VPC peering + private link for full isolation.
[00:03:48] Dev: can we mandate mTLS for dedicated instances?
[00:03:52] Priya: yes, dedicated and private have mTLS options and customer-managed certs. For Redwood-hosted we recommend mTLS to customer endpoints where possible.

[00:04:30] Sofia: HSM import — what's the flow if we want to import an external key into Redwood's HSM connector? we can't export private key material.
[00:04:38] Priya: correct, you don't export. Two options: 1) you keep the CMK in your cloud KMS and Redwood uses KMS APIs to do Wrap/Unwrap operations (recommended), 2) you use an HSM import token for our on-prem connector where the private key material is generated within your HSM and we reference it via an importer — the importer never transfers the raw key to Redwood.
[00:05:00] Miles: we'll provide an HSM import checklist — sample IAM roles, allowed crypto primitives, and entropy requirements.

[00:05:47] Liam: audit logs — we need immutable logs of who called unwrap/rotate/disable keys and we need those logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[00:05:56] Priya: Redwood exposes key-access audit events as part of our platform logs. We can stream them to your CloudWatch / Stackdriver / SIEM via a secure forwarder and sign them; logs include requestor identity, operation, model route, and request context.
[00:06:12] Nora: are those logs tamper-evident? We need forensics-proofing, chain-of-custody for investigations.
[00:06:18] Priya: we support log signing and append-only storage options; for highest assurance you can ship logs to an external WORM store or immutable S3 with account-level locks. We also sign each log batch with an internal signing key you can verify.

[00:07:05] Dev: on RBAC — how granular can we be? we want role segregation between ops, developers and security auditors.
[00:07:12] Jordan: Redwood integrates with SSO (SAML/OIDC) and SCIM for provisioning. Roles map to key policies and we support just-in-time elevated access with MFA enforced for key operations like unwrap/rotate/export metadata.
[00:07:30] Sofia: is there a separation of duties enforcement? for example, the person who triggers a rotation can't approve key export.
[00:07:36] Priya: yes, key policies plus the platform's RBAC enforce that. We also have approval workflows for sensitive ops; you can require two-person approval for key export or for emergency unseal.

[00:08:20] Liam: let's talk incident runbook. If a key is suspected compromised, what's the immediate steps and how do we limit customer impact?
[00:08:28] Priya: our recommended runbook: 1) revoke the CMK (disable in KMS) so new unwrap calls fail; 2) issue a fallback plan — Redwood can automatically route to a pre-provisioned fallback key/version for minimal read-only operations while you rotate; 3) run a forensic snapshot: collect logs, capture KV cache snapshots (if allowed) and record sequence numbers to reconstruct any decrypted outputs.
[00:08:54] Miles: important note — revocation affects new operations; anything already decrypted in-memory may still be accessible until processes are restarted. We recommend a fast process to redeploy runtime shards to flush memory.
[00:09:10] Dev: what's expected downtime for full rotation?
[00:09:13] Jordan: depends on scale — in our tests with dedicated pools, a rolling key rotation with cache flush and shard restart is ~8-12 minutes for a small fleet, but can be longer for large clusters. We'll run drill to measure for your topology.

[00:10:05] Nora: legal also asked about key escrow — if we die, will Redwood hold an escrowed copy?
[00:10:12] Priya: Redwood doesn't retain unwrapped customer keys. For escrow scenarios we can support customer-managed escrow: a split-key escrow where you deposit an encrypted recovery blob in a controlled escrow service, or a multi-party escrow with an HSM provider. We'll document options.

[00:10:48] Sofia: data residency — some models and logs must stay in EU. Can we pin region and ensure keys never leave region?
[00:10:55] Miles: yes, with private deployment or dedicated regional capacity you can pin both data and keys to a region. For BYOK, ensure the CMK is regional and you disable cross-region key replication. We'll include region scoping in the architecture diagram.

[00:11:30] Liam: one of our concerns — rollback and forensics after a suspected exfil. How do you provide evidence that model outputs were not leaked?
[00:11:38] Priya: we capture request/response hashes, model route IDs, and can replay request traces against a known-good model snapshot. Combined with signed logs and deterministic randomness seeds, you can produce reproducible outputs for investigation. There's limitations but it helps narrow scope.

[00:12:22] Dev: about key rotation frequency — minimum recommended cadence?
[00:12:27] Jordan: industry best practice is at least annual CMK rotation, data keys rotated more frequently depending on risk (e.g., daily for ephemeral workloads). But this is workload dependent. We'll discuss a policy template.

[00:13:10] Sofia: can we do an automated rotation without impacting inference latency? our SLOs are strict.
[00:13:16] Miles: we support asynchronous key rotation where new data keys are generated and used for new encryptions, while old keys remain for decryption until a scheduled migration. For low-latency paths we recommend staged rotation and warming caches. Also Redwood Optimize can recommend batching/QoS to keep latency within SLOs during rotation windows.

[00:14:00] Liam: compliance — SOC 2 and ISO questions: can you provide the reports and the scope includes encryption controls and incident response?
[00:14:07] Jordan: yes, we'll share SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 coverage, and we can provide attestation letters describing controls for crypto and incident response.

[00:14:35] Nora: one more — auditability for delegated customers, like partners who access certain models. How do you isolate keys per tenant?
[00:14:42] Priya: tenancy isolation is handled via key namespaces: each tenant gets a logical key wrapper and separate key policies. Cross-tenant access is prevented by policy and enforced in the runtime.

[00:15:10] Dev: show of hands — do we want Redwood to manage rotation or do it ourselves?
[00:15:15] Sofia: we'd prefer control but want Redwood to support automation and runbooks.
[00:15:21] Liam: same. We need clear SLAs for rotation and emergency support.

[00:15:50] Miles: operationally, here's a proposed runbook (high level):
 - Detect: SIEM alert or Redwood anomaly -> create incident ticket
 - Contain: disable CMK or apply deny policy to stop new unwraps
 - Fallback: route traffic to fallback key/version to preserve read-only operations
 - Eradicate: rotate keys, flush caches, restart runtime shards
 - Recover: validate integrity, resume normal ops
 - Lessons: post-mortem with signed logs and artifacts

[00:16:35] Nora: for forensics, what artifacts will Redwood provide?
[00:16:40] Priya: signed access logs, per-request metadata, request/response hashes, snapshot of active KV cache metadata (not plaintext without permission), and a timeline of control-plane events.

[00:17:20] Jordan: request — we'll run a key rotation drill in staging with your SREs to measure impact. Proposed date 2026-12-09.
[00:17:28] Sofia: that works, we'll confirm.

[00:17:45] Liam: legal wants indemnity language around key custody — we will need to review contract language if Redwood holds any recovery material.
[00:17:52] Jordan: understood. Our standard enterprise contract has BYOK clauses; we'll surface the escrow options and related liability items.

[00:18:30] Dev: curious about performance overhead when calling a remote KMS for every unwrap — do you recommend local cache of wrapped keys?
[00:18:36] Miles: yes, we recommend a small, secure in-memory cache of unwrapped data keys per process with short TTLs and rotation. For high QPS paths we use the cache plus asynchronous pre-warm to avoid KMS throttling.

[00:19:10] Sofia: what about key derivation for per-shard keys?
[00:19:14] Priya: we support hierarchical key derivation: CMK -> data key -> session key. Derivation functions are HMAC-based and documented; we can provide the spec.

[00:20:02] Liam: audit question again — what timezone stamps are used in logs? we need UTC and local region mapping.
[00:20:08] Priya: all logs are UTC by default and include region metadata. We can also include customer-defined timezone mappings in the forwarder.

[00:21:00] Jordan: quick recap then next steps.
[00:21:05] Jordan: recap — Ember wants BYOK across AWS and GCP, strong forensic logging, regional residency for EU models, two-person approvals for export, and a key-rotation drill. Actions: Jordan share SOC2/ISO docs; Priya share HSM import checklist and key policy template; Sofia provide list of environments; schedule drill for 2026-12-09.

[00:21:26] Sofia: yep, will do.
[00:21:30] Liam: thanks all. Any final questions?
[00:21:34] Nora: none from compliance.
[00:21:36] Dev: no.
[00:21:40] Jordan: great, we'll follow up via email with attachments and a calendar invite for the drill.
